chapters.title: Chapter 5 — The Wife Who Died Young

spans.text: The iron gate of his grandmother's house was the same iron gate Sami had pulled at since he was nine and tall enough to reach the upper hinge. The hinge still caught at the same place. He lifted at the catch with his thumb the way she had taught him, and the gate swung in against the lemon tree.

It was July and not yet four o'clock. On the rue Mongi Slim the shutters had been closed since two and would not open again until after six. On the walk from the Centre a small boy on a bicycle had said sahha to him without looking up, and Sami had said it back, and the greeting had landed in the part of his hearing that did not catalogue. He catalogued the not-cataloguing as he turned into his grandmother's street.

The lemon tree had a fruit on the south branch that had set the previous month and was not yet yellow. The tiled court was swept. The olive sapling she had brought back from her sister's house in 2019 stood in its clay pot in a small square of shade. He stepped high over the kitchen threshold, which had been reset one finger higher in the second winter Amalia had lived here without his grandfather, when the back wall was repointed.
The kitchen smelled of coffee. She had heard the gate and had put the briki on.
Tata,
he said. He used the Greek for her without thinking about it.
Sami,

she said. She did not turn from the stove. She would turn when the foam had reached the rim and not before. He set the shoulder bag carefully on the cane-seated chair against the kitchen wall, because of the recorder inside it, and stood at the table and watched her watch the foam.
Sit down,
she said.
Don't stand at me.

He sat. The table was the table where she had taught his great-aunt at four and her own daughter at four and him at six. The chair on the court side was hers. The chair on the kitchen side was for whoever she had decided would be there that afternoon, and he had been at the kitchen side since he was small. He did not know whether the rule was a rule or a habit she had not noticed enforcing.

She poured the coffee into two small cups and added orange-blossom water to her own from the glass bottle on the shelf beside the candle. She did not add it to his, because he had told her at sixteen that it was not for him. She had remembered for sixteen years.
The candle on the shelf was lit, which it was not always. He noticed it without remarking on it.
She sat down across from him.
Eight times,
she said.
Eight times.
With today you will have heard the song eight times this summer.
Three times for the recording. Four times before that.
And today is the fourth time for the recording.
The fourth time. Yes.
Why so many.
He looked at her. She was waiting.
For the lemon tree,
he said.
She made the small sound at the back of her throat that he had heard her make in place of a laugh since he was nine.
For the lemon tree,

she repeated, with the slight French rise at the end of the verb that she had inherited from her grandmother and that neither her daughter nor he had inherited, though he could hear it when she did it.
The leaves,
he said.
The leaves are loud today.
The leaves are correct today.
She made the sound again.
Put your recorder near the door,
she said.
I will sing for the lemon tree.

He took the recorder to the small wooden stool by the kitchen door: a flat black machine with the cardioid head he had brought back from a conference in Lyon two summers ago. He pointed the head into the court at the angle that held the lemon tree on the right and the kitchen on the left in equal balance, pressed the button at the side, and watched the level settle. He could hear the bottom of his grandmother's breathing at the level the head was reading, which meant the leaves would come through clean.
It is recording,
he said.
Allez,

she said, in French, without looking up from her coffee. She had begun every session this way. He had never asked why she switched to French to begin. He had come to think of it as the small permission she gave herself to begin in a language none of the three women who had taught her the song had begun in, so that the beginning was hers.
He came back to the table and sat across from her and did not look at the recorder. Looking at the recorder during a take was the surest way to lose what the take was for.
She began.

She sang the first verse in the unhurried voice she always sang it in, the melody low in her throat and never moving far from where it began. The Greek of the song was not the Greek she spoke at the table and not the Greek the parish read on Sundays. It was the Greek a Kalymnian woman would have sung in the 1890s, before the sponges were gone and the men with them. The Arabic word that came in at the end of the third line was a word he had never heard outside this song from this woman. He had asked her at twenty-two what it meant and she had said it meant nothing now, which was her way of telling him that she had asked her own mother and her own mother had told her the same.
She came to the chorus. The chorus was the counting line. She counted the saints.
She counted them in the order she had counted them at the table when he was six and in every session since. He had never written the order down. The recorder was writing it down now.

Each name took the same small breath at its end before the next. The breath between the seventh and eighth names was the same length as the breath between the third and fourth. It was the rhythm of something counted to keep it counted, not to dress it.

The second verse was the one about the women at the door of the church when the men had not come back. It had no count. There her voice went briefly into the register her parish had trained, which was not the register of the song or of the table. The two registers did not blend in her throat. The verse worked because the seam between them was where the women at the door had stood.
She counted the saints again, in the same order.
She came to the third verse.

She had told him at the beginning of the summer that the song was three verses, not two; that her mother had not always sung the third; and that she, Amalia, had decided some years ago that she would sing the third whenever she sang the song. She had not said why. He had noticed that she always gave herself one small extra breath before it, as if to remember that she had decided to sing it.
She gave herself the breath. She sang the third verse.

It was about a road and a saint's day and a woman walking. The Arabic word at the end of its second line was the same word he had asked her about at twenty-two. The verse ended with a small turn back toward the counting chorus.
She counted the saints.
A neighbor's radio two houses down played a Tunisian melody at very low volume, which the cardioid head would either take or not take and which he would decide about at the desk that night.
She came to the seventh name. The seventh was a saint whose day fell in October in any calendar a Greek-Orthodox-trained ear had been taught. She gave the name its breath. She moved to the eighth.
The eighth name was a saint whose day fell in August.

His hands stayed where they were on the table and his face did not change, because his face had been trained not to change at a kitchen table since he was nine. August after October was not the order of the liturgical year, or of the parish year, or of any year he had ever read. He had heard the eighth name in this same place in every session before today, and he had not heard it. He had heard the count as count. He had not heard the count as sequence.

He heard the ninth name and the tenth and the eleventh, and the order went on as she had always sung it, and the order was an order, and the order was wrong, and it was the only order she had ever sung it in.
The display flickered as the level rose past his threshold, because she pushed slightly on the eleventh name, as she always did. The level dropped back to the line.

She sang the twelfth name. The melody returned to the low place it had begun in, and the breath after the twelfth was the breath she had taken to end the song at the table when he was six. She added nothing. She drank a little of her coffee, which was cold now.

He waited the twelve seconds the head needed for a clean tail of ambient. Then he went to the door and stopped the recorder. The take was forty-one minutes and twelve seconds. He would write it on the index that night.
Tata,
he said, coming back to the table.
Thank you.
Eight times,
she said.
Eight times,
he said.

She poured them both a small fresh measure from the briki, which she had put back on the flame without his noticing. He thanked her in Arabic; she thanked him in Greek. The trade was old enough that they no longer marked it.
You are still hearing it,
she said.
He looked at her.
The song. Even with the recorder on. You hear it for the recording and you hear it for the lemon tree. Sometimes you hear it for me.
I hear it for you.
Good.

She looked at the candle on the shelf. It had burned down a finger's width during the take. She lit it on the days she decided to, and the days were not the days the parish calendar marked; he had known that since he was twelve. He had never asked which saint the candle was for. The not-asking had become, across twenty years, the way he honored that there was a saint and that the saint was hers.
Bring me the recording on the small machine,
she said.
I want to hear it once before you put it in the file.
I will.
You don't have to. Only if you want to.
I want to.

She nodded once and finished her coffee and did not get up. After twenty-three years of leaving this table at the end of an afternoon, he understood that she was waiting for him to go, and that the waiting was the form her permission took.
He picked up the bag. At the kitchen door he looked back. She was looking at the lemon tree through the door of the court.
Khalas,
he said.
Pige na doulepseis,
she said. Go and work. She had told him to go and work since he had begun to know what work was.
He crossed the court, pulled the gate open at the catch, and closed it behind him. The hinge caught at the same place.

He walked toward his apartment off the Avenue Habib Bourguiba with the bag against his hip. He had what he had come for: the eighth session, the clean ambient take, the lemon tree audible, his grandmother's voice unhurried, and the count in the order it had been counted to her at four.
At home he set the bag down by the desk and stood for a long moment with his hand on it, and did not yet take the recorder out.
The eighth name had been the eighth name in eight sessions. He had not heard it as a question until today.

The apartment had two windows on the avenue side and one on the courtyard. Sami had chosen it in his second year at the Centre because the courtyard window opened onto a wall painted the pale ochre Sfax wall paint of his childhood, and he paid for the wall with the noise of the avenue.

The desk faced that window. It was a kitchen table he had carried up the stairs from a shop on rue Mongi Ali in 2017: on it the recorder, the headphones, a stack of three green-covered transliteration notepads, a black pen, a blue pen, a water glass, a lamp with a paper shade. The lamp was on. The avenue-side window was open four fingers, because the building did not breathe across the apartment in July unless the avenue side was open at least four fingers and the courtyard side all the way. He had eaten a piece of bread at the door before he sat. He did not remember eating it.

He opened the topmost notepad to a new page and wrote, in the small careful hand he had used since he was twelve: eighth session, 22 July, 16:42 to 17:23, courtyard kitchen, lemon-tree ambient, cardioid head door-mounted, level clean. He underlined it once. Below it: transliteration, verse three chorus, names.

He pulled the headphones on, and the world went small and close. He could hear the avenue through the foam of the left earcup, faintly, the way a man can hear through a wall that there is a man on the other side of it.

He had a rule: no transliteration until he had listened to a take three times. The first listen was for the rhythm. The second was for the syllables. The third was for what was not said. He had not arrived at the rule as a theory. He had arrived at it through the first elder he ever recorded, a Greek-Tunisian widow in her eighties at La Marsa who had sung him a wedding song, and whose take he had transliterated on the train back to Tunis with the confidence of a man who believed his ear was sufficient. Two weeks later, listening slow, he found that what he had taken for one word was two, with a small intake of breath between them that he had missed because he had been writing. After that he never wrote on the first listen. The counting became method, and the method became the private rule by which he treated his elders as he had been taught at his grandmother's table to treat them.

He let the third verse run, pen capped. He heard the small extra breath before it. He heard the Arabic word at the end of the second line, and felt the small reach of his own throat toward it, the body's memory of standing at that same table at six while his grandmother sang him the song for the first time and reached for the same word in the same way.
The verse turned toward the chorus. He counted in his throat without sound, not naming the saints, only counting them.
One. Two. Three. Four. Five. Six. Seven. Eight. Nine. Ten. Eleven. Twelve.

He stopped the playback at the closing breath. The page was still blank below the underlined line. He refilled his water glass at the tap. Through the courtyard window the wall was holding its ochre as the dusk came down.
The second listen was for the syllables.

He uncapped the black pen and wrote each name as he heard it, syllable by syllable, in the Latin-script transliteration he had developed so the names would be searchable later by a researcher who did not read Greek. He wrote them down the left margin, one to a line, numbered, in the order she sang them. The fourth he had to take twice. He came to the eighth and wrote it in the same careful hand, looked at it, and moved on. Ninth, tenth, eleventh, twelfth.
Twelve names in the order she had sung them.
The third listen was for what was not said.

He did not put the headphones back on yet. He uncapped the blue pen and, down the right side of the page, wrote beside each name the saint's day his ear had been trained to assign it. He checked the fourth against the small pocket calendar he kept in the desk drawer and corrected it by one day. He checked the seventh because the seventh saint was observed on three octaves across the year in Sfax and he wanted the one the parish kept. The seventh fell in October. The eighth fell in August.

In the left column, the name as she had sung it. In the right, the day his ear assigned. Between the seventh and the eighth ran the same small horizontal stroke of his ruler that separated every line on the green page from the next.
He sat with the line.
Then he finished the column and read the dates down the page.

January for the first name. April for the second. June for the third. February for the fourth. September for the fifth. December for the sixth. October for the seventh. August for the eighth. November for the ninth. March for the tenth. May for the eleventh. January for the twelfth.
He read them three times.

It was not the liturgical year. In the Patriarchate of Alexandria calendar his grandmother's parish followed, the year began on the first of September and ran through the eight feasts of the Mother of God and the cycle of named days any Greek-Orthodox boy could rehearse from his catechism. It was not the parish-Sfax order either, which put the patronal days of the Sfax community at the front of any list a community elder would draw up. And it was not the order a Kalymnian woman of 1890 would have given, because the names were not all Kalymnian and the cluster around the Aegean patronal days was not the cluster on the page.
The order was an order. The order was Amalia's. The order was not random.
He read the dates a fourth time, against his own rule of three. The fourth reading was the one he allowed himself when the third had not told him what he needed.
January, April, June, February, September, December, October, August, November, March, May, January.

He counted the intervals between the named days. January to April: three months. April to June: two. June to February: eight, counting forward across a year. February to September: seven. September to December: three. December to October: ten, counting forward. October to August: ten. August to November: three. November to March: four. March to May: two. May to January: eight.
Three. Two. Eight. Seven. Three. Ten. Ten. Three. Four. Two. Eight.

He wrote the eleven numbers at the bottom of the page below the column. They were not the numbers of the liturgical year or of the parish cycle or of any cycle he had read. They were a sequence, and the sequence was Amalia's: the order she had sung eight times this summer, the order she had sung to him at six, and, if the song lived in her body the way she said it did, the order her mother had sung to her at four.

He capped both pens and took the headphones off. The avenue was at the hour after the shops closed and before the cafes filled, the hour of a few car horns and the call of a peanut vendor on the corner two blocks down.

He thought about who he could call. Marina in Athens. Eleni in Sydney. Lysandra, whose number he had at the bottom of a file in the second desk drawer and had used twice in his life. The parish council office across the avenue from the Centre, where Yannis Trikalinos sat most mornings of the week with the donation ledgers in a cabinet to which he had not granted Sami access. His grandmother.

He did not call anyone. He had a column of twelve names, a column of twelve dates, and a row of eleven intervals, and he had the engineer's certainty that the order was not random and the recording engineer's discipline of not naming a pattern he did not yet have the frame to name. He made a glass of mint tea and turned the page.
On the fresh page he wrote: index entry, eighth session, 22 July. Below it: speaker: Amalia Ben Youssef-Kouris, b. 1947, rue Mongi Slim, Sfax.

It was the first time the hyphenated name had gone down on a project page in his own hand. The index used the speaker's birth name in full as the speaker gave it when consent was taken. Amalia had given the hyphenated form at the first session in May, at the kitchen table, over the consent form he had drawn up in Arabic and French because she had asked for both. She had said the hyphen was for the part of her that was her father and the part that was her mother, and that she had used it since she was twenty, when she began her own household. Her mother had been born a Kouris and she had married a Kouris cousin, so the second half of the hyphen was her mother's name and her husband's at once.

He looked at the name on the page. He thought of the iron gate and the candle on the shelf and the chair on the court side of the table that was hers and the chair on the kitchen side that was his. He thought of her mother, whom he had never met, and of her mother's mother, who had not lived to see her oldest grandchild old enough to ask about her. He thought of the small extra breath she gave the third verse.
He wrote: language: Greek (family-affection register, Kalymnian-emigrant 1890s inflection), Arabic (household and song-internal), French (sessional opening, civic register).
He wrote: song: family counting song, three verses, twelve-name saint's-day chorus.
He did not write cipher. He did not have the frame. He wrote instead: order of chorus names notable; see green notepad p. 1, eighth session transliteration.
The tea had gone cold by the time he drank it. The dusk had taken the ochre out of the wall.
He turned back to the column and read the numbers once more.
Three. Two. Eight. Seven. Three. Ten. Ten. Three. Four. Two. Eight.

He did not yet know what the numbers were the address of. He knew only that a count kept this carefully inside a song was a count that pointed somewhere, and that someone had wanted both the place and the pointing kept. A count was not a keepsake. A count was a set of directions, and a thing that needed directions hidden inside a child's song for eighty years was a thing that had been put somewhere and not retrieved.

He thought of his grandmother at her own table with her own coffee, which she would have made at eight, as she had made the eight o'clock coffee since his grandfather stopped being in the house. He did not think she had taught him the song to ask him to do anything with it. She had taught him the song because it was what she had been taught, and the teaching was the form the keeping took. The third listen had told him that what was not said was the frame for the order. The frame was somewhere outside the song, in a place the song pointed at without naming, the way Amalia pointed at the candle by not naming the saint, and the way she had pointed at Yannis Trikalinos, the second time he had ever asked her about him, by not naming whatever it was Yannis carried.

He went to the courtyard window. Somewhere in the building a radio was playing what he thought was the same Tunisian melody he had heard from two houses down at his grandmother's that afternoon. He listened to it, and listened to himself listen.

He thought of Marina, who had told him once over coffee at a conference in Athens that she had begun to treat any pattern in an archive that was too clean as a pattern someone had wanted to be found. He thought of Eleni, whom he did not know well, but whose certified Pearl Ledger excerpt he had been waiting two weeks for a courier to deliver. He thought of Lysandra, whom he barely knew.
He did not call any of them.

He set the recorder to sleep, left the notepads on the desk with the index page open, and washed the tea glass and set it upside down on the cloth by the sink. In bed he counted the months without moving his lips, three two eight seven three ten ten three four two eight, and stopped after the third time, because the discipline held in the dark as it held at the desk. The apartment had its night quiet: the avenue side at the hour after the cafes had filled and before they emptied, and the courtyard side, which was the quiet of the wall.

Before he slept he thought of the candle on the shelf. For twenty years he had not asked which saint it burned for. Now the eighth name in the column and the candle in his grandmother's kitchen had stopped being separate facts.
